title: Do Large Language Models Add Value in Credit Investing? Evidence from a Disclosure-Reading Agent for US Bank Bonds
abstract: We ask whether a large language model, reading only public regulatory disclosure, can identify credit deterioration in US banks-regional banks in particular-before it is priced into the issuer's corporate bonds, a setting far less studied than equities. Using SEC filings and FDIC bank financials, and holding the agent strictly away from market prices, we assess twenty-three banks each quarter over a decade. On data from after the model's training cutoff, the agent flagged a specific funding deterioration at a regional bank two quarters before its spread widened sharply, reading deposit stress in the disclosure that the reported ratios did not yet show. We then backtest a simple strategy built on the signal. The paper's central methodological contribution is its treatment of contamination in pretrained models: because such a model may already have absorbed an issuer's filings, news and eventual outcome, we separate genuine point-in-time reasoning from embedded knowledge through post-cutoff testing and anonymisation, and we report what these controls can and cannot remove.
why: Real LLM for credit deterioration, out-of-sample, handles model contamination.

title: Enhanced Government Financial Oversight: Reducing Fraud with AI and Metadata Analytics
abstract: Federal agencies routinely receive clean audit opinions, yet reported fraud and improper payment losses remain substantial. This report argues that the gap is structural rather than a failure of audit execution. Conventional financial audit relies on sampling, manual review, and documentation testing, methods designed for a paper-based transaction environment and poorly suited to the volume and velocity of digital federal payments. The report proposes supplementing financial audit with metadata analytics. Metadata is generated automatically for every federal transaction and captures timing, routing, approval sequence, vendor identifiers, and system-level attributes that conventional audit evidence does not examine. When metadata is paired with machine learning classifiers, auditors can test entire transaction populations rather than samples, and can surface anomaly patterns that sampling-based procedures are structurally unable to detect. Experimental testing reported here shows that AI-driven metadata analysis substantially outperforms conventional sampling in fraud detection rates, with improvements of up to sevenfold in the configurations tested. The report sets out how agencies can operationalise this approach within existing audit standards and organisational structures. Three recommendations follow. First, incorporate metadata analysis into federal financial management and audit processes. Second, launch controlled AI pilot programmes within agencies to build capability and validate models against known cases. Third, redefine financial audit objectives so that oversight shifts from retrospective opinion-issuing toward real-time protection of taxpayer funds.
why: Fraud detection proposal without empirical results shown.

title: Generative AI and Investment Decision-Making Does AI Improve Investor Information Processing and Portfolio Decisions?
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is rapidly becoming an information intermediary, analytical assistant, and decision interface in financial markets. This paper asks a central question: does GenAI improve investment decision-making by reducing information-processing frictions, or does it create new behavioral and systemic risks that can offset those gains? The paper develops an integrated framework linking GenAI use to five stages of the investment process: information acquisition, interpretation, belief formation, portfolio construction, and post-decision monitoring. It synthesizes recent evidence from retail-investor behavior, analyst research, portfolio advice, experimental finance, and market microstructure. The emerging literature suggests that GenAI can lower search and interpretation costs, expand the breadth of information considered, improve some forms of forecast accuracy and risk-return matching, and broaden access to sophisticated analytical tools. At the same time, interactive AI can increase perceived competence without commensurate improvement in underlying skill, amplify persuasion, transmit model biases, generate false or stale claims, and promote portfolio convergence when many investors consume similar machine-generated narratives. The paper therefore rejects a binary "AI versus human" framing. Its central proposition is that investment outcomes depend on the architecture of human-AI collaboration: grounded retrieval, source verification, calibrated uncertainty, suitability constraints, independent risk controls, and preservation of heterogeneous judgment. A multi-method empirical agenda is proposed, including randomized experiments, brokerage-account analysis, portfolio backtests, event studies, and market-level tests of convergence, liquidity, and price efficiency. The resulting framework predicts that GenAI is most beneficial when it functions as a decision-support system that compresses information and improves discipline, and most hazardous when it becomes an unverified decision substitute. The paper concludes with implications for investors, asset managers, broker-dealers, investment advisers, regulators, and designers of AI-enabled financial systems.
why: Perfect topic but explicit rejection: literature review/synthesis, not methodology.

title: Artificial intelligence, grid congestion, and capital accumulation
abstract: This paper develops a dynamic general equilibrium model in which conventional capital and AI/data-center capital share a congestible electricity grid whose installed capacity cannot expand faster than a technological ceiling permits. When data-center capital is more grid-intensive, competitive firms allocate too much private capital to the AI sector, and a Pigouvian charge on grid load equal to the marginal congestion damage restores the efficient allocation for a given grid stock. If AI-driven growth exceeds the maximum feasible rate of grid expansion, the ceiling binds and the congestion elasticity enters the long-run growth rate: growth becomes constrained by the rate at which complementary infrastructure can scale. The model also distinguishes AI productivity from data-center energy efficiency. The former raises grid use by expanding the scale of the economy rather than by economizing on grid capacity. The latter generates a macroeconomic rebound equal to the ratio of the congestion elasticity to the labor share; consequently, the engineering saving systematically overstates the reduction in grid load delivered by efficiency improvements.
why: Macro theory, grid congestion; not actionable for practitioners this quarter.

title: From Vulnerability to Resilience: The Non-Linear Role of Green Finance and Generative AI in G7 Climate Adaptation
abstract: Research has shown that green finance has an impact on carbon emissions and a pervasive role in sustainable development; yet studies on the green finance impact on broader climate vulnerability remain scarce, particularly regarding the moderating role of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI). Therefore, this study investigates the non-linear impact of green finance on climate vulnerability and the moderating role of GenAI within G7 economies from 2000-2024. To ensure that the results are reliable and policy insights are well-informed, cross-sectional dependency, non-stationarity and distributional heterogeneity are addressed using robust and relevant methods. Considering the role of dynamic capabilities and the EKC hypothesis in the framework, our findings indicate that green finance has a non-linear relationship with climate vulnerability, confirming inverted U-shape. In the early stages, green finance may increase vulnerability, but upon reaching the threshold, it helps reduce vulnerability. GenAI weakens this early negative effect by improving the efficiency of green finance, helping economies achieve climate resilience at a lower level of green finance. Moreover, ESG readiness, energy productivity and institutions play a favorable role for climate resilience while urbanization, and income play a detrimental role in climate resilience and adaptation objectives. Policy makers in the G7 economies may reflect on executing actions to support modern technologies including GenAI, expanded green financial mechanisms, enhancing business readiness, strengthening institutions and their capacity building, and energy improvements to effectively reduce climate vulnerability, achieve sustainable economic growth, and build climate resilience.
why: Green finance climate study, AI is moderating variable.

title: AI-Agent Adoption Readiness in Emerging-Market Finance Functions: A Structural-Constraints Framework for Mid-Market Bangladeshi FMCG Finance Teams
abstract: Agentic AI is increasingly marketed as a near-term standard for corporate finance, yet a persistent gap exists between adoption ambition and actual deployment even among well-resourced firms in developed markets. This gap is widely attributed to data infrastructure and governance shortfalls, an assumption embedded in most commercial AI-agent product design. This paper asks whether that assumption holds in a mid-market, emergingeconomy setting by examining AI-agent adoption readiness among Bangladeshi FMCG finance functions. Using a desk-based, qualitative research design, the paper develops the Mid-Market AI-Agent Adoption Readiness (MAAR) framework, a five-criterion diagnostic scoring Data Infrastructure Maturity, Integration Cost Tolerance, Regulatory Readiness, Talent Availability, and Existing Digitization Level on a 1-to-5 scale grounded in the Technology-Organization-Environment framework. Applying MAAR to public evidence on four multinational-affiliated FMCG firms operating in Bangladesh (Unilever Bangladesh, Unilever Consumer Care, Marico Bangladesh, and Reckitt Benckiser Bangladesh) finds that Regulatory Readiness, not Data Infrastructure Maturity, is the most binding constraint, driven by an active central-bank restriction on inputting confidential data into commercial AI tools and the near-total absence of firm-level AI governance policy. This finding inverts the assumption underlying most global AI-agent vendor design and implies that a viable adoption pathway for this market must treat regulatory and governance clearance as a gating first step rather than a downstream formality. The paper contributes a reusable, evidence-grounded readiness framework and a phased adoption pathway for finance leaders, AI vendors, and policymakers operating in similarly underregulated emerging markets.
why: Framework paper, desk-based, qualitative, no data or implementation path.

title: Governing in the Gap: The EU AI Act Deferral, the Non-Life Blind Spot, and the Sixteen-Month Window for Insurance Regulators in Emerging Markets
abstract: On 27 July 2026, Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, the Digital Omnibus on Artificial Intelligence, entered into force, amending the EU Artificial Intelligence Act days before its general application date. The Regulation deferred the core Chapter III requirements for standalone high-risk AI systems under Article 6(2) and Annex III from 2 August 2026 to 2 December 2027, a revised timetable intended to align obligations with the availability of implementation support, including harmonised standards, guidance, and conformity assessment arrangements. This paper offers an early insurance-specific analysis of the deferral and makes three contributions. First, it maps the regulatory position of insurers as at August 2026, identifying an asymmetric application phase in which transparency obligations and the Act's governance and enforcement architecture apply while the substantive Annex III high-risk regime remains deferred. Second, it examines the scope asymmetry of Annex III, which expressly identifies AI intended for risk assessment and pricing in relation to natural persons in life and health insurance, while non-life underwriting, claims triage, fraud detection, and reserving are not expressly enumerated, despite carrying much of the weight of actuarial AI deployment. Third, it asks what emerging-market insurance regulators should learn from a benchmark jurisdiction that deferred its own timetable on the eve of application. Drawing on comparative supervisory approaches in Switzerland, the United States, and Ghana, and on the author's Trust-First framework of institutionally contingent technology adoption, the paper proposes a standards-readiness sequencing model gating application dates on norm availability, supervisory capacity, and market infrastructure. The deferral, the paper argues, is not free time but a governance window.
why: Regulatory policy analysis, no research contribution.

title: RELIABILITY-AWARE MACHINE LEARNING FOR PREDICTIVE RISK MANAGEMENT IN CRITICAL INFRASTRUCTURE OPERATIONS
abstract: The increasing use of machine learning (ML) for predictive risk management in critical infrastructure presents significant opportunities for anticipating threats, supporting operational planning, and strengthening system resilience. However, infrastructure decision-making involves consequences that extend beyond conventional measures of predictive accuracy, particularly when decisions are made under changing, uncertain, or disrupted operating conditions. This study employs a systematic critical literature synthesis and conceptual framework development approach to examine research addressing predictive analytics, data reliability, critical infrastructure, cybersecurity, uncertainty, machine learning, adaptive decision-making, and resilient operations. The synthesized findings indicate that the reliability of ML-based risk predictions can deteriorate when data quality declines, operational contexts shift, cybersecurity disruptions affect information or systems, or models encounter conditions beyond their effective operating boundaries. The findings further demonstrate that model confidence alone is insufficient for determining whether a predictive risk assessment is reliable enough to support consequential infrastructure decisions. Accordingly, the study develops a reliability-aware predictive risk management perspective in which data reliability, model reliability, contextual reliability, operational conditions, security reliability, and uncertainty collectively influence decision reliability and adaptive decision authority. The proposed framework emphasizes continuous reliability assessment, context-sensitive interpretation, and adaptive human-AI decision-making as essential mechanisms for strengthening the trustworthiness and resilience of AI-supported critical infrastructure operations.
why: Infrastructure reliability review, not finance-specific or novel.

title: Measuring GEO Visibility: Prompt Corpora Define the Answer Market A Critical Survey of Validity, Partial Identification, and Source Attribution
abstract: To measure the visibility of a source or brand in a generative engine’s answers, a set of prompts is submitted to the engine, and displayed sources, citations, or mentions are recorded according to specified rules. These observations are aggregated into a GEO (generative engine optimization) visibility score. The choice of prompts determines which situations are evaluated; the weights determine their relative importance in the calculation. We call this weighted set of answer opportunities an “answer market.” This constructed market does not necessarily represent actual user demand. Prompt wording can alter document retrieval, the sources brought into competition, and the answers produced. Once these answers have been generated, calculating the visibility score requires identifying the source appearances, citations, or mentions of interest. If this task is assigned to a language model, a second instruction enters the process: the instruction telling the model how to evaluate the answers. This instruction can change the scoring even when the evaluated answers remain identical. Our critical survey examines how these choices help define what a GEO score measures. It draws on research that examines whether the indicators used measure the intended phenomenon, as well as research on total survey error and information retrieval evaluation. The proposed framework makes explicit the evaluated situations and their annotation, prompt formulations, execution conditions, weights, and scoring rules. Two calculations illustrate the consequences of these choices. Using published aggregate rates from three selected subcorpora in Grossman et al., two weighting schemes yield generative-answer activation rates of 39.7% and 70.5%, without changing the rates within each subcorpus. These results concern whether a generative answer appears; they do not measure brand visibility. A fictional example shows that reweighting can reverse the ranking of two systems when each performs better in different categories of situations. When weights are unknown or remain to be chosen, the framework proposes reporting a set of admissible scores. It distinguishes two approaches: determining the values compatible with the data and assumptions about a target population, which concerns partial identification; and examining how the score varies across weighting conventions, which concerns normative sensitivity. The presence of a citation is insufficient to establish a source’s contribution to an answer. To examine this contribution, the article defines a comparison between answers produced with and without a source in a controlled documentary context. It distinguishes this contrast from an intervention on the full engine in the presence of competing sources. Together, these contributions provide a framework for interpreting GEO scores, supported by reproducible calculations. No new experiments are reported; the general empirical validity of the proposed protocol remains to be assessed.
why: Brand visibility optimization, entirely off-topic to finance.

title: A Cross-Scale Physics-Based Proton Exchange Membrane Fuel Cell Plant Model for Flexibility Valuation in Hydrogen-Powered Hyperscale Data Centers
abstract: AI-driven hyperscale data centers are accelerating demand for secure on-site power, but planning for hydrogen-powered proton exchange membrane fuel cell (PEMFC) plants still relies largely on static efficiency curves that cannot capture how partial-load operation changes hydrogen use, recoverable heat, and flexibility value. Here we develop a cross-scale, physics-based PEMFC plant model that resolves cell-level activation, ohmic, and mass-transport losses and propagates them to plant-scale hydrogen, electricity, and heat metrics. Electrochemical parameters calibrated on a 114-kW automotive dataset transfer to a 1-MW stationary system with low calibration error (4.38% stack-voltage MAPE and 0.95% net-power MAPE). Applying this model to a 500-MW facility, annual hydrogen use per unit of electricity is essentially unchanged across three annual demand profiles: baseline, seasonal, and 100 h/yr curtailment (~56.3 kg-H2/MWh; spread below 0.1%), whereas the marginal hydrogen intensity during curtailment is ~14% higher. This gap is small relative to annual fuel expenditure but material for design decisions. Annual thermal rejection is comparable in magnitude to delivered electricity (~0.88 MWhₜₕ/MWhₑ), but the modeled coolant temperatures are too low for direct reuse above 40 °C without heat upgrading. The results identify where annual-average curves suffice (annual fuel planning) and where physics-based marginal quantities are required (flexibility pricing, delivery-infrastructure sizing, and feasibility screening) for hydrogen-powered hyperscale data centers.
why: Fuel cell physics, not finance or financial ML.
